## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 88 (*Tūlonaddha*) governs the prohibition against constructing monastic furniture stuffed or upholstered with cotton (*tūla*) [Hüsken 1997]. According to the rule, a monk who makes or has someone make a bed or chair with luxurious upholstery must strip off the upholstery before confessing the offense [Hüsken 1997]. Ute Hüsken classifies this precept as an *uddālanaka-pācittiya* ("involving tearing off/pulling down"), an offense requiring the physical dismantling of the prohibited covering from the bed or seat in addition to confession, analogous in form to *nissaggiya pācittiya* regulations and to *chedanaka* (cutting down) or *bhedanaka* (breaking) rules [Hüsken 1997]. Lambert Schmithausen highlights the motivation presented in the rule's background narrative, noting popular criticism that upholstering a couch with cotton reflects a lack of compassion because it entails harming living beings [Schmithausen 1991]. In discussions of early Buddhist bodily comportment and institutional regulation, Michael Radich cites Pācittiya 88 among rules curtailing indulgence in excessively luxurious or stuffed furniture [Radich 2007].

In the Theravāda tradition, the rule corresponds to Bhikkhu Pātimokkha Pācittiya 88, Parivāra Bhikkhu Pācittiya 88, and the nuns' equivalent rule, Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 164 (also in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and Parivāra) [Clarke; Hüsken 1997]. Complete parallels are attested in the Vinayas of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṅghika, and Dharmaguptaka traditions in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan recensions, as well as the Kāśyapīya and Upāliparipṛcchā traditions. DharmaNexus records 362 internal Pali text-reuse matches across 96 texts, showing extensive formulaic sharing with surrounding rules—especially Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiyas 87, 89, 90, 91, and 92, and Nissaggiya Pācittiyas 12, 19, 21, and 26—and aligns portions of the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya parallels [DharmaNexus].
